explanations.answer: On the Sabbath and the New Moon
explanations.explanation: Sabbath and New Moon, friend. The Lord GOD says the gate stays shut six days, “…but on the Sabbath day and on the day of the New Moon it shall be opened.” So the work week keeps it closed, and those two days swing it wide.

explanations.answer: On Passover and the Day of Atonement
explanations.explanation: Those are big days, friend, but this verse doesn't name them. The Lord GOD names two days for the east gate: the Sabbath and the New Moon. Everything else in the work week, that gate stays shut.

explanations.answer: At the start of every harvest
explanations.explanation: I'd love a gate that opens whenever the harvest does, but harvest isn't mentioned here. The Lord GOD says the gate is shut during the six days of work. It opens on the Sabbath day and on the day of the New Moon.
The priests, friend. The prince stands by the gatepost, and they're the ones who sacrifice his burnt offerings and peace offerings. He brings the offerings and they handle the altar work.

Elders are respected folks, but they aren't the ones named here. The text says the priests sacrifice the prince's burnt offerings and peace offerings. The prince just stands by the gatepost while it happens.
Prophets don't show up in this verse, friend. It's the priests who sacrifice the prince's burnt offerings and peace offerings. The prince stands by the gatepost and watches them work.
He bows in worship, right at the threshold of the gate. Then he departs. I think that's a humble way for a prince to head out the door.
Nothing in this verse has the prince reading anything out loud. The text says he bows in worship at the threshold of the gate and then departs. Short and simple, friend.
The verse never has him blessing a crowd. What it says is that he bows in worship at the threshold of the gate and then departs. The bowing is the whole moment.

I get why it sounds right, friend, but the gate stays open longer than that. The text says the prince departs, and then adds, “…but the gate must not be shut until evening.” (Ezekiel 46:2) So the prince leaves, and the gate stays open.
False, friend. The prince bows and departs, but the gate stays open. The text says, “…but the gate must not be shut until evening.” (Ezekiel 46:2) No slamming it behind him.
The people of the land, friend. On Sabbaths and New Moons they also bow in worship before the LORD at the entrance to that gateway. So it's not just the prince bowing. Everybody gets to worship.
Nobles aren't named here. The text says the people of the land bow in worship before the LORD at that gateway entrance. That's everyday folks joining the prince on the Sabbaths and New Moons.

Judges don't appear in this verse, friend. The text says the people of the land are also to bow in worship before the LORD at the entrance to that gateway. The prince and the people worship on the same days.
South gate, friend. The text says whoever enters by the north gate must go out by the south gate. And it works the other way too: in by south, out by north. Everybody exits by the opposite gate.

That's the one gate he doesn't leave by. The text says no one is to return through the gate by which he entered. So the north gate worshiper heads out the south gate, and each must go out by the opposite gate.
The east gate is a different gate, friend. Here the text only talks about the north and south gates. A worshiper who enters by the north gate must go out by the south gate.

True, friend. The text says, “When the people enter, the prince shall go in with them, and when they leave, he shall leave.” So he walks in with the crowd and walks out with the crowd. No sneaking out early for him.
It's actually true, friend. The text says, “When the people enter, the prince shall go in with them, and when they leave, he shall leave.” He goes in with them and leaves when they leave.
True, friend. For the prince's freewill offering, “…the gate facing east must be opened for him.” He offers it just as he does on the Sabbath day. Then he goes out, and the gate is closed.
It's actually true, friend. The text says that when the prince makes a freewill offering, the gate facing east must be opened for him. After he goes out, the gate is closed.

Descendants, friend. If the prince gives a gift to one of his sons as an inheritance, it will belong to his descendants. It becomes their property by inheritance. So the gift stays in the family line.
Brothers aren't mentioned here. The text says the gift to a son will belong to his descendants. It becomes their property by inheritance.
Neighbors don't get it, friend. When the prince gives a son an inheritance, it belongs to that son's descendants. It's their property by inheritance, and that's the end of the line.

explanations.answer: It goes back to the prince
explanations.explanation: Back to the prince, friend. A gift from his inheritance to a servant belongs to that servant until the year of freedom. Then it reverts to the prince. A son's gift stays with the family line, but a servant's gift goes back.

explanations.answer: It passes to the servant's sons
explanations.explanation: That's how it works for the prince's sons, but not for a servant. The text says the gift belongs to the servant until the year of freedom. Then it reverts to the prince.
The priests don't get it here, friend. The text says a gift to a servant belongs to that servant until the year of freedom. Then it reverts to the prince.

I can see why it might sound like the prince has that kind of power, friend, but the text says the opposite. The prince must not take any of the people's inheritance by evicting them from their property. He's to provide for his sons from his own property.

False, friend. The text says, “The prince must not take any of the inheritance of the people by evicting them from their property.” He gives his sons an inheritance from his own property. The people's land is theirs.

explanations.answer: So none of His people are displaced from their property
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the Lord GOD gives, friend. The prince provides for his sons from his own property, “…so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.” The rule is about the people staying put on their land.

explanations.answer: So the prince's sons never argue over who gets the land
explanations.explanation: That's a tidy idea, friend, but the text doesn't give that reason. The Lord GOD says the rule is “…so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.” It's about the people keeping their land.

explanations.answer: So the land around the temple can keep growing larger
explanations.explanation: Nothing in the verse mentions the land growing, friend. The Lord GOD says the prince provides from his own property “…so that none of My people will be displaced from his property.” That's the stated reason.
Cooking offerings, friend. The man says the priests will boil the guilt offering and the sin offering there, and bake the grain offering. It's a kitchen spot in the priests' holy chambers.
There's no treasure in this verse, friend. The man says it's where the priests shall boil the guilt offering and the sin offering, and bake the grain offering. It's for cooking.
Gatekeepers aren't mentioned here, friend. The man says it's the place where the priests shall boil the guilt offering and the sin offering. They also bake the grain offering there.

True, friend. The man says the priests cook those offerings there “…so that they do not bring them into the outer court and transmit holiness to the people.” So the cooking happens in the holy chambers, and the outer court is kept clear of it.
It's actually true, friend. The man says the priests boil and bake there “…so that they do not bring them into the outer court and transmit holiness to the people.” That's the reason the text gives.
